summary: Documents how the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard have been satisfied by BGP. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is the report card showing BGP passed the tests needed to move up a level.

what is the mib for bgp
subtitle: How BGP has performed in real-world deployments and why it meets Draft Standard criteria

tldr.problem: For BGP to advance from Proposed Standard to Draft Standard, the Internet standards process required demonstration of multiple independent interoperable implementations and successful operational experience under real-world conditions.
tldr.mechanism: Three independent implementations (cisco, gated, and NSFNET) were deployed operationally since 1989 across multiple production networks (CA*Net, NSFNET T1, NSFNET T3, CICNET, MERIT, PSC). Operational experience with 56 border routers spanning 7 autonomous systems proved BGP's stability and performance in diverse environments.
tldr.outcome: BGP demonstrated that it meets all general and Draft Standard requirements: it has proven implementations, handles the full spectrum of protocol features including authentication and loop suppression, and has shown superior performance compared to the older EGP protocol.

today: RFC 1266 is an Informational RFC documenting BGP's readiness for standardization. BGP has since been standardized and has become the universal routing protocol for connecting autonomous systems on the Internet.

sections.title: Proving BGP Ready for Draft Standard
sections.content:
This RFC documents operational experience with the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) to show that the protocol meets the requirements for advancement to Draft Standard status. The Internet standards process requires not just theoretical analysis but evidence of real-world deployment.

The RFC is the second of two reports on BGP. The first (RFC 1265) provided performance analysis. This RFC documents experience: multiple independent implementations, successful deployment in production networks, use of all significant protocol features, and operational data comparing BGP to the older EGP protocol.

BGP Version 2 removed the restrictive "up," "down," and "horizontal" relationship model from Version 1 and introduced path attributes. Version 3 made minor refinements including lifting restrictions on the NEXT_HOP attribute and adding the BGP Identifier field to the OPEN message.
sections.eli5: This report shows that BGP has been used in real production networks and has proven it works well enough to become an official standard.

sections.title: Three Interoperable Implementations
sections.content:
The RFC documents three completely independent, interoperable implementations of BGP:

Cisco: Developed wholly by Cisco, running on Cisco's proprietary operating system for its routers.

Gated: Developed by Jeff Honig (Cornell) and Dennis Ferguson (University of Toronto), running on multiple Unix variants (4.3 BSD, AIX, etc.). This is the only publicly available open-source BGP implementation, and implementation experience with gated has been documented in RFC 1164 to help other implementers.

NSFNET: Developed by Yakov Rekhter (IBM), running on NSFNET backbone infrastructure.

The existence of these three independent, interoperable implementations, each taking about 1 man-month of development effort, demonstrates that the protocol is well-defined and implementable. The RFC notes this satisfies the IAB/IESG requirement for Draft Standard status.
sections.eli5: Three different organizations wrote working versions of BGP without copying from each other, and they all could talk to each other, proving the protocol is clear enough to implement from scratch.

sections.title: Production Deployment and Coverage
sections.content:
BGP has been in production use since 1989 across multiple large networks:

CA*Net: 10 border routers in a ring topology over 56 Kbits/sec links (heavily congested).

NSFNET T1 Backbone: 20 border routers on T1 lines.

NSFNET T3 Backbone: 15 border routers on T3 lines.

NSFNET T3 Test Network: 7 border routers.

CICNET, MERIT, PSC: 1-2 border routers each.

In total, 56 border routers spanning 7 autonomous systems run BGP, with 49 of those routers across 6 autonomous systems in the operational production Internet. The full set of exterior routes carried by BGP exceeds 2,000 networks.

This deployment covers heterogeneous link speeds (56 Kbits/sec to 45 Mbits/sec), diverse router hardware (from slow PC/RT to high-performance RS/6000), both special-purpose routers (Cisco) and general-purpose Unix workstations, and diverse topologies (sparse rings, dense backbones).

BGP is used for exchange of routing information between transit and stub autonomous systems, and between multiple transit networks. In CA*Net, T3 NSFNET Backbone, and T3 NSFNET Test Network, BGP carries all exterior routing information exclusively.
sections.eli5: BGP has been running on real backbones and regional networks for two years, handling over 2,000 networks, working reliably in slow and fast links and different kinds of routers.

sections.title: Feature Coverage and Security
sections.content:
Operational experience exercised all basic features of BGP protocol, including authentication and routing loop suppression.

BGP provides flexible and extensible security mechanisms. All BGP sessions are authenticated based on the BGP Identifier of the peer and the autonomous system number advertised. The protocol allows carrying encrypted digital signatures in every BGP message. All authentication failures trigger sending a NOTIFICATION message and immediate connection termination.

Because BGP runs over TCP and IP, its security can be augmented by authentication mechanisms provided by TCP or IP.

A BGP Management Information Base (MIB) has been published for network management, with 27 objects covering BGP peer connections and received path attributes.
sections.eli5: BGP has proven it can authenticate peers, prevent routing loops, support encrypted signatures, and integrate with network management systems.

sections.title: The TCP Transport and Convergence Issues
sections.content:
Some members of the IETF expressed concern about BGP's use of TCP as transport, particularly regarding convergence speed. Operational experience identified one real issue: slow convergence in the presence of severe network congestion on CA*Net (56 Kbits/sec congested ring topology).

Analysis showed this is not a problem with BGP or TCP: any routing protocol has difficulty when packets carrying routing information are dropped due to congestion. Replacing TCP would not prevent congestion-related packet loss, since the transport has no control over routers dropping packets.

The operational solution proven effective is to mark BGP packets with IP precedence or a well-known port number and configure routers to try not to drop marked packets. CA*Net's experience shows this completely solves the convergence problem.

Notably, the convergence behavior of BGP under extreme congestion is comparable to the steady-state behavior of EGP under normal conditions. Within an AS, interior gateway protocol (IGP) convergence is far more critical and sensitive to packet loss than BGP.

The RFC recommends that every routing protocol should clearly specify how congestion affects behavior and what mechanisms avoid negative effects.
sections.eli5: People worried about BGP being slow to adapt to network changes, but tests showed the real problem was network congestion, not the protocol itself, and marking important packets solved it.
